title: प्रथमोनुवाकः
samhita: अध्य॑वोचदधिव॒क्ता प्र॑थ॒मो दैव्यो॑ भि॒षक् । अहीग्॑श्च॒ सर्वा᳚ञ्ज॒म्भय॒न्-थ्सर्वा᳚श्च यातुधा॒न्यः॑ ॥
pada: अधीति॑ (अधि॑) । अ॒वो॒च॒त । अ॒धि॒-व॒क्तत्य॑धि = व॒त्का। प्र॒थ॒मः । दैव्यः॑ । भि॒षक । अहीन॑ । च॒ । सर्वान॑ । ज॒म्भयन्न॑ । सर्वा᳚: । च॒ । या॒तु॒-धा॒न्य॑ इति॑ यातु = धा॒न्य॑: ॥
krama: अध्य॑वोचत् । अ॒वो॒च॒द॑धिव॒क्ता । अ॒धि॒व॒क्ता प्र॑थ॒मः । प्र॒थ॒मो दैव्यः॑ । दैव्यो॑ भि॒षक् । भि॒षगिति॑ भि॒षक् । अहीग्॑श्च । च सर्वा᳚न् । सर्वा᳚ञ्जम्भयन् । ज॒म्भय॒न्-थ्सर्वा᳚न् । सर्वा᳚श्च । च यातुधा॒न्यः॑ । या॒तु॒धा॒न्य इति॑ यातु-धान्यः ॥

sayana.text:
May that Rudra, who is the 'adhivakta'—one who is capable of speaking for me first, saying "this one is superior"—may he speak (adhyavochat) thus. If he says I am superior, then my superiority is established at once. Therefore, may such a Rudra speak for me. What kind of an advocate? 'Prathamah'—chief among the gods. 'Daivyah'—worthy of all gods; the meaning is he is capable of protecting the gods himself. 'Bhishak'—the physician; because by the mere meditation on him, all diseases are pacified, he is a healer. Doing what? Destroying all serpents (ahin)...
...



...all of them, like serpents, tigers, etc. And all the 'yatudhanis'—destroying (jambhayan) even all the races of Rakshasas (demons). (6)

bhatta_bhaskara.dhyana: "One should meditate on the three-eyed Lord, who has the crescent moon on his crown, who is the enemy of Time (Kala), who has serpents as his sacred thread, and who is like blazing fire." (6)
bhatta_bhaskara.text:
For 'Adhyavochadadhivakta', the metre is Anushtup. Some say Nichrit. The Rishi is Kanva. The Deity is Shambhu. These four mantras starting from here are in the third person (parokshakrita). 'Adhyavochat'—let him speak for (us). The past tense is used in the sense of the imperative in the Veda. 'Adhivachanam' means a speech that is superior or elevated. It means speaking with partiality (favor). As in "one should speak for a Brahmin." Or, it means speaking with lordship or superiority; may he speak for us devotees. 'Adhivakta' means one whose nature is to speak for others; or one who is always capable of speaking for his devotees. Those who are not lords, if they speak for others, become objects of laughter. He states the reason for his being an advocate: 'Prathamah'—the foremost, the chief. 'Daivyah'—existing among the gods. Or, 'devana' (from which 'deva' is derived) means play, desire for conquest, business, light, praise, or movement. He is the form of joy in play; the form of victory in the desire for conquest; the form of clarity in business; the form of light in illumination; the form of the object of praise in hymns; and the form of the destination or the form of wind in movement. Or, the gods are those endowed with divine knowledge; he is the foremost among them. 'Bhishak'—physician. He is the healer of afflictions (vyasana) like disease, heat, and worldly existence. There is another mantra: "I hear you are the physician of physicians." 'Bhishak' can also mean he who makes fear perish, or he who is reached by the mind in the midst of fear, because he is the ground of fearlessness. Or, he who graces through the breaking of the body (of ego). Doing what should he speak for us? He says here: 'Ahimmshcha sarvan jambhayan'—by means of destroying. 'Jambhanam' means destruction. 'Ahayah' are those who come and harm beings; those whose nature is to strike, the direct killers of subjects like tigers, serpents, scorpions, etc.—destroying all of them. The word 'cha' (and) should be seen after 'all', meaning 'destroying all of them indeed'. And all the 'yatudhanis'—destroying all the races of Yatudhanas (sorcerers/demons). 'Yatus' are the sorrows or the illusions that cause pain; 'Yatudhanas' are those in whom these reside. This is what is said: may he speak for us while destroying all those who wish to strike, like scorpions, tigers, thieves, etc., and those who are not peaceful.
...

14  

...destroying all those who are ready to kill directly, and those who cause pain secretly through magic, like Rakshasas, Pishachas, etc., as well as diseases like epilepsy (apasmara), etc. May the God speak for us, saying "Do not fear, I will protect you."

Now for the Purashcharana of this mantra: having performed half-Krichhra penance, and for five days thereafter eating only vegetables, roots, and barley porridge, and chanting continuously while not opposing necessary daily duties, one completes the Purashcharana. Then, let a king have protection (raksha) performed with this. For the protection of all, one should offer eight thousand oblations of white mustard (shveta-siddhartha), rice, Durva grass, and barley, soaked in ghee, into one's own fire or a churned fire, as in daily rites. Specifically for the king, ten thousand oblations. In that same fire, offering eight thousand oblations of charu mixed with sesame, jaggery, barley, and milk, the king becomes long-lived. At all times, one should give Dakshina (fees). Dakshina is of three types: distinguished by the best, medium, and lowest. Ten thousand gold Nishkas is the best Dakshina. Five thousand is medium. Three thousand is lowest. Or, three hundred is best, two hundred is medium, and a hundred Nishkas is lowest.

"In whatever rite a Dakshina is prescribed as part of the ritual, first one should give that Dakshina, and then the Dakshina for the ritual part."

Thus, one should give Dakshina at all times. Or, sixty-four is best, thirty-two is medium, and twenty-four is the lowest. In rites with many performers, the best should be given to each person. In a rite with a single performer, to that one alone. Furthermore, they cite:

"A sacrifice with too little Dakshina destroys the sacrificer."

Kings and those equal to them should give the best Dakshina. Others should give medium, etc.

"He who, while having wealth, out of delusion performs the ritual without the proper extent (of Dakshina), his mind being overcome by greed—he does not obtain the fruit of that rite."

In a rite with ten performers, a thousand should be given as Dakshina. In a rite with five or four performers, five hundred. In a rite with one performer, three hundred. For the Acharya (preceptor), double. The Acharya should be thought of as the Lord Himself. At all times, such Dakshina should be given. There, one should place a mantra-pot (kalasha) near the fire. Placing the mantra-pot in front of the fire, one should establish a pot made of gold or silver. Having invoked the God in that fire, one should perform the homa in his presence. At the end of the homa, one should sprinkle the king with the water from the pot. The king who always honors his Guru becomes especially protected. With this same (mantra), if one is going on a path near an anthill, having consecrated cotton seeds, salt, and white mustard eleven times, he should throw them in directions other than the one he is going. Then he should proceed while chanting, purified. He is freed from tigers, thieves, Brahma-rakshasas, Yakshas, ghosts, etc. With this same (mantra), another method for destroying disease is told—a sick person, having consecrated white mustard seeds seven times, should tie and keep them in his tuft (shikha); health will ensue. By white mustard seeds used thus, one is freed from Kumara-grahas (afflictions of children) etc. Having consecrated a Pala (measure) of dry ginger...
...



...having thrown (ginger) into milk and boiled it, one should offer eight thousand or eight hundred oblations for oneself and drink the remainder. All diseases vanish.

abhinava_shankara.dhyana: Meditation on Lord Maheshvara with resplendent Goddess.
abhinava_shankara.text:
The divine healer (daivya-bhishak), foremost among those who speak
        on behalf of [their devotees], has declared this — destroying all
        serpents and all evil spirits (yatudhanyah).

— Even though in this way [the Lord has been] propitiated through salutation
and praise, [one might wonder:] how would the averting of misfortunes [caused
by] Yama (the god of death), the unrelenting and fierce ones, and other
terrible [beings] and other gods [who are] instruments of [fulfilling the results
of] the wicked person's sins — how would their [influence] be removed? Not
knowing this, [the devotee] now desires to know the path for its removal,
[realizing] that all these [other gods] are helpless and without any capacity
[to act] independently — this is stated:

"Adhy abocat" — adhivacana means speaking on behalf of, championing
[someone's cause], as [confirmed by] the Brahmana: "yad brahmano 'shajjagad
prathameyatam brahmanaya chivruyat" (whenever a brahmin goes before the
world, he should declare [the cause of the brahmin]). The meaning here is as
follows: adhivakta — He who is of the nature of championing the devotees'
cause, that is, foremost and supreme; daivya — He who exists among the gods,
in the sense of the indwelling controller of the gods (devantaryami-artha);
bhishak — the physician of all suffering, the healer of all the afflictions of
worldly existence such as disease and others. [This is confirmed by] the Shruti:
"bhishaktamam tva bhishajam shrinomi" (I hear that You are the greatest
physician among physicians). Such a Lord adhy abocat — has declared [His
stance] on behalf of [His devotees], "chandishi lungi" — in the optative [the
aorist is used in the sense of optative], meaning He makes a declaration
of partisanship for His devotees. What does He do [while declaring this]?
While destroying (sambhayan, annihilating) all ahi-s (snakes, and other visible
harms such as thieves and tigers), and all yatudhanya-s — classes of yatudha-
ja (evil spirits); rakshas, pishachas, and other invisible assailants — adhy
abocat, He has declared [His protection].

Here, the objection might be raised: "How can the Lord, who is impartial
toward all, make a partisan declaration in your favor? Doesn't this lead to
the charge of partiality (vaishanya) on His part?" To counter this, the word
adhivakta is used — the declaration on behalf of devotees is motivated by
their act of devotion; therefore it does not bring any defect upon the Lord.
"Vaishanya-nairghrnye na sapekshatvat" (partiality and cruelty do not apply
to the Lord, because His actions are conditioned [by devotees' karma]) —
such is the principle, as stated in the Vedanta.

Even though the Lord champions [His devotees'] cause, one might ask: how
can the suffering resulting from the workings of Yama and other independent
deities not occur? To dispel this doubt, the word prathama (foremost) is
used. [The Lord is described as] "yo devanam prathamah purastadavikarako
rudro maharshih" (the foremost of the gods, pre-eminent, Rudra the great seer);
"tameshvaranam prathamam maheshvaram tam daivatam prathamam ca daivatam"
(the first among lords, the great lord, the first among divinities and the
foremost divinity); "yo devah sarvadeveshu mahadeva iti smritah, tasmai
namastuh kurvana divi tishthanti devatah" (the God who is known among all
gods as Mahadvea — the gods who salute Him dwell in heaven) — such [texts]
from the Shruti, Smriti, Itihasa (epics), and Purana establish that the Lord is
supreme among all gods. Since He who champions [His devotees'] cause is
foremost [among all gods], there is no scope for the fear of suffering inflicted
by subordinate gods.

Not only [freedom from] suffering caused by other gods, but also the supreme
status of being worshipped by all gods [is obtained by the devotee] — because
the Lord, by virtue of being the indwelling controller (antaryami) of all those
[gods], the singular deity who champions [the devotee] became the one whose
favor is sought — this is indicated by [the word] "daivyah," which alludes to
His quality of being the indwelling controller of all gods.

By the word "bhishak" (physician), using the analogy of the physician as
described in the Shiva Purana — "just as a physician who knows the cause of
illness causes harm to the patient through treatment like surgery, cauterization,
and so on, yet in doing so heals him — there is no cruelty here, only
compassion" — the supreme compassion of the Lord is set forth. And through
this, even while striking the ahis (serpents and evil forces) and yatudhanyahs,
His compassion toward even those [beings] is shown. Just as a wound-physician
(vrana-vaidya, a surgeon), though momentarily causing pain through surgery,
cauterization, and the like, ultimately brings happiness to the patient by
healing his wound and is thus compassionate — likewise, the Lord who is the
physician of worldly existence (samsara-vaidya), even while striking the ahis
and yatudhanyahs, by removing the sins that are the root cause of their
future [suffering] and making them pure, progressively leads them to happiness
— therefore His compassion is not diminished. This [meaning] is shown here.

Since He [acts] while declaring [His protection] — not [merely] praying "may
[the Lord] destroy" — [and since] the phrase "adhy abocat" (He has declared)
rather than "jambhayatu" (may He destroy) shows the Lord's faultless
sovereignty — and since [in this mantra] the destruction of the ahis, yatudhanyahs,
and the deities that impel them (such as Yama) is attributed to the Lord Himself
acting independently — and since the Lord, having first protected the devotee
by destroying the ahis and yatudhanyahs, when [other] gods come and ask
"how is this sinner to be protected?" makes the partisan declaration "This one
is mine — how does he have sins?" — this is the sequence. Hence even for
great sinners — having destroyed the messengers of Yama who were about to
take them, like hunters and others, through his own emissaries, when Yama,
Chitragupta, and others report the incident to the Lord and He has them
brought to Kailasa — [the Lord says:] "Even if inadvertently, these performed
acts such as throwing bilva leaves [at Shiva's image] and prostrations; therefore
they belong to Me, and you have no authority over them." Such stories are
repeated frequently in the Puranas. With this understanding, the fact that in
this [mantra] "raksha ca no adhi ca deva bruhi" (protect us, and also champion
our cause, O God) — protection comes first and the declaration of partisanship
second — is to be comprehended. This is why this mantra is the remover of all
afflictions from serpents, Vishnu [adversaries], rakshasas, pishachas, and
all [such beings]. Hence its designation as a kavacha (armor/protective mantra)
— as stated by the revered Bodhayana: "adhy abocat iti kavacham" (the mantra
'adhy abocat' is the armor).

[Continuing the commentary on the sixth mantra "adhyabocat..."]

Those who are fierce, relentless, and unvanquishable — the servants of
Yama and other deities — and those who are instruments of delivering the
fruits of that wicked person's sins, [as well as] other gods — how would
the averting of their [inflicted] misfortunes be possible? Not knowing this,
the [devotee] desires to know the remedy; [the Lord] declares that all of
them are incapable and powerless [on their own]:

"adhyabocat" — adhivacana is speaking in favor of, championing [a cause]:
as [confirmed by] the Brahmana, "when a brahmin goes before the world,
he should declare [the cause of the brahmin]." The meaning here is: He who
is by nature an adhivakta (advocate, champion) of devotees — that is,
foremost and supreme; daivya — dwelling among the gods, meaning the
indwelling controller of the gods; bhishak — the physician, the healer of
all the afflictions of worldly existence such as illness and others. [As the
Shruti says:] "bhishaktamam tva bhishajam shrinomi" (I hear You are the
greatest physician among physicians). Such a Lord, adhy abocat — has
proclaimed [His partisanship]. What does He do [while proclaiming]?
Sambhayan — destroying all ahis (serpents and other visible assailants
including thieves and tigers) and all yatudhanyah — classes of yatudha
beings; those who are invisible assailants like rakshasas, pishachas, and
others — while destroying them, He has proclaimed [His protection].

Here, [if one objects:] "How can a Lord who is the same toward all make
a partisan proclamation in your favor? Does this not lead to partiality
(vaishanya)?" — to dispel this objection, the word adhivakta is used.
The Lord's declaration on behalf of devotees is motivated by the devotees'
act of devotion; hence it brings no fault upon the Lord. "Vaishanya-
nairghrnye na sapekshatvat" (partiality and cruelty do not apply, because
of [the Lord's actions being conditioned by] devotees' actions) — such is
the principle here.

Even though the Lord champions [His devotees'] cause, there might be the
fear: "will not the suffering resulting from the actions of Yama and other
independent deities still occur?" To remove this doubt, prathama (foremost)
is used: [scriptural passages confirm the Lord's supremacy:] "yo devanam
prathamah" (He who is foremost among gods); "tameshvaranam prathamam
maheshvaram" (the foremost of all lords, the great Lord); "yo devah
sarvadeveshu mahadeva iti smritah, tasmai namastuh kurvana divi tishthanti
devatah" (the gods known among all gods as Mahadeva — those who
salute Him dwell in heaven). Since the one who champions [the devotee's
cause] is the foremost of all gods, there is no room for fear of suffering
caused by subordinate gods.

Not only [freedom from] suffering caused by other gods, but [the devotee
also attains] the status of being worshipped by all gods — because, by
virtue of the Lord being the indwelling controller (antaryami) of all those
gods, the singular supreme deity who has become a partisan advocate [of
the devotee] — this is indicated by the word "daivyah," which implies the
Lord's quality of being the indwelling controller of all gods.

Through the word "bhishak" (physician), and through the analogy of the
physician from the Shiva Purana — "a physician who knows diagnosis causes
harm to the patient through surgery, cauterization, and the like, but here
there is no cruelty; compassion alone motivates him" — the supreme
compassion of the Lord is expressed. And thereby, even while striking the
ahis and yatudhanyahs, His compassion toward even those beings is implied.
Just as a surgeon (vrana-vaidya), though momentarily causing suffering to
the wounded through surgery and cauterization, yet heals the patient's
wounds and thus brings happiness — and is therefore compassionate — so
too the Lord who is the samsara-vaidya (physician of worldly existence),
even while striking the ahis and yatudhanyahs, by removing the sins that
are the cause of their future birth and thus purifying them, progressively
brings them to happiness — therefore His compassion is not diminished.

[The text shows that:] since He declares [His protection] — saying "adhy
abocat" (He has declared), not "jambhayatu" (may He destroy) — the Lord's
faultless sovereignty is demonstrated. Not the manner of a subordinate who,
incapable of subduing the ahis and yatudhanyahs himself, propitiates them
and intercedes for the devotee saying "please spare this one who is mine"
— but rather: Himself capable, first protecting the devotee by destroying
the ahis and yatudhanyahs, [then] when the gods come asking "how should
this sinner be protected?", making the partisan declaration "This one is
mine — what sin does he have?" — hence even great sinners [are protected].
Stories of hunters and others whose Yama-messengers were destroyed by the
Lord's divine emissaries, and who were brought to Kailasa, and to whom
Yama and Chitragupta reported their deeds — and to whom the Lord replied:
"Even if inadvertently, these have performed acts such as throwing bilva
leaves [at My image] and prostrations; therefore they are Mine and you
have no authority over them" — such stories are repeatedly told in the
Puranas.

With this understanding, in this mantra "raksha ca no adhi ca deva bruhi"
(protect us, and then champion our cause, O God) — protection comes first,
then the declaration of partisanship — this is the sequence shown. Thus
this mantra is the remover of all afflictions from serpents, rakshasas,
pishachas, and all other beings. Hence its designation as a kavacha
(armor/protective formula) — as stated by the revered Bodhayana:
"adhyabocat iti kavacham" (the mantra 'adhyabocat' is the protective armor).

Even though the Lord champions [His devotees'] cause, one might ask:
how can the suffering resulting from the workings of Yama and other
independent deities not occur [for the devotee]? To dispel this doubt,
the word prathama (foremost, primary) is used. [Scriptural texts confirm:]
"yo devanam prathamah purastadavikarako rudro maharshih" (Rudra, the
great seer, who is the foremost and pre-eminent among gods); "tameshvaranam
prathamam maheshvaram tam daivatam prathamam ca daivatam" (the first
among lords, the great lord, the first among divinities and the foremost
divinity); "yo devah sarvadeveshu mahadeva iti smritah, tasmai namastuh
kurvana divi tishthanti devatah" (the God who is known among all gods
as Mahadeva — the gods who offer salutation to Him dwell in heaven).
Such texts from the Shruti, Smriti, Itihasa, and Purana establish that the
Lord is the supreme among all gods. Since the Lord who champions [His
devotees'] cause is the foremost [of all gods], there is no room for fear
of suffering inflicted by subordinate gods.

Not only [freedom from] suffering caused by other gods, but also the
supreme status of being worshipped by all the gods [is attained] — because
by virtue of the Lord being the indwelling controller (antaryami) of all
those [gods], the one Lord who has become a partisan advocate [for the
devotee] is the sole supreme deity — this is shown by the word "daivyah,"
which implies the quality of being the indwelling controller of all the gods.

Through the word "bhishak" (physician), using the analogy of the physician
as set forth in the Shiva Purana: "A physician who knows the diagnosis
causes harm to the patient through surgery, cauterization, and the like;
yet here there is no cruelty — compassion alone motivates him." With this
analogy, the supreme compassion of the Lord is expressed; and by this,
His compassion even toward the ahis (serpents) and yatudhanyahs whom He
destroys is demonstrated. Just as a surgeon (vrana-vaidya), though causing
the wounded patient momentary pain through surgery and cauterization, yet
heals his wounds and thereby brings him happiness — and is thus
compassionate — so too the Lord who is the physician of worldly existence
(samsara-vaidya), even while striking the ahis and yatudhanyahs, purifies
them by removing the sins that are the root cause of their further births,
and thereby progressively leads them to happiness — therefore His
compassion is not diminished.

The fact that [the text says] "adhy abocat" (He has declared, He has spoken
on behalf) rather than "jambhayatu" (may He destroy) shows the Lord's
faultless sovereignty. Not that He, being incapable of subduing the ahis
and yatudhanyahs Himself, propitiates them with a request: "spare this one
who is mine" — on the contrary, [He is perfectly capable:] He Himself first
protects the devotee by destroying the ahis and yatudhanyahs, and when
the [other] gods come asking "how is this sinner to be protected?", He
makes the declaration "This one is mine — what sin does he have?" Hence
the procedure [shown in this mantra applies] even to great sinners.

Stories are recounted in the Puranas: hunters and others, [though sinners,]
were saved by the Lord's divine emissaries who killed the messengers of
Yama who had come to take them; brought to Kailasa, when Yama,
Chitragupta, and others reported [the sinners'] deeds to the Lord, He
declared to them: "Even if inadvertently (yad ricchaya), these performed
acts such as throwing bilva leaves [at My image] and prostrations — therefore
they are Mine; you have no authority over them." Such stories are repeatedly
narrated in the Puranas. Understanding this, the sequence in this [mantra]
where "raksha ca no adhi ca deva bruhi" (protect us, and then champion
our cause, O God) places protection first and the partisan declaration
second — this is its import. Hence this mantra is the one that removes all
afflictions from serpents, rakshasas, pishachas, and all [such beings].
This is why Bodhayana calls it a kavacha (protective armor): "adhy abocat
iti kavacham" (the verse 'adhy abocat' is the armor mantra).

[Continuation of the commentary on the sixth mantra "adhyabocat..."]

— by removing the sins that are the cause of their future births and thus
purifying them (making them pure, anagha), He progressively leads them
to happiness — therefore His compassion is not diminished.

[The text shows that:] since He [acts] declaring His protection through
"adhy abocat" rather than praying "jambhayatu" (may He destroy) — the
Lord's blameless sovereignty (nirdosham ishvaratvam) is demonstrated.
It is not that, being incapable Himself of subduing the ahis and yatudhanyahs
and the deity of death (mrityu-devata) who impels them, He propitiates them
with the request "this person who is mine should not be harmed" — thus
supplicating the ahis and yatudhanyahs and freeing the prostrated devotee
by such intercession — [the Lord does not act in that manner]. Rather,
being perfectly capable Himself, He first protects the devotee by destroying
the ahis and yatudhanyahs; and then, when the gods come asking "how is
this sinner to be protected?", He makes the partisan declaration: "This one
is mine — what sin does he have?"

Hence [this applies] even to great sinners: hunters and others, whose Yama
messengers were destroyed by the Lord's own divine emissaries (shiva-duta)
as they were being led away; and when they were brought by the Supreme
Lord to Kailasa, and Yama, Chitragupta, and others reported the incident
to the Lord — He said to them: "Even if inadvertently (yad ricchaya),
they performed acts such as throwing bilva leaves [at My image] and
prostrations — they are mine; therefore you have no authority over them."
Such stories are repeatedly proclaimed in the Puranas.

Understanding this intent, in this [mantra] — "raksha ca no adhi ca deva
bruhi" (protect us, O God, and then champion our cause) — protection
(rakshana) comes first, and the declaration of partisanship (adhivacana)
comes afterward. Thus this mantra is the one that removes all afflictions
from serpents, rakshasas (demons), pishachas (spirits), and all [such
beings]. This is precisely why its designation is kavacha (armor, protective
formula) — as stated by the revered Bodhayana: "adhyabocat iti kavacham"
(the verse 'adhy abocat' is the armor).

[End of the sixth mantra of the first anuvaka of Shri Rudra Bhashyam.]

58                    

The seer (ṛṣi) of this mantra is Kaṇva, the metre (chandas) is Anuṣṭup, and the deity (devatā) is Śaṃsu. [The dhyāna-śloka for meditation is:] "One should meditate upon the three-eyed Lord (trilochana), who is adorned with a digit of the moon, who bears a serpent as his sacred thread, and who is resplendent like blazing fire." The purascaraṇa (preliminary consecration) is accomplished by reciting [the mantra] forty-five thousand times. Thus [ends] the sixth [mantra].
